title: Шеф уезжает, а туристы приезжают  (The Chef Leaves and the Tourists Arrive)

segments.t: Having secretly replaced the spoiled snails with contraband ones, Max assures Chef Barinov that the stock in the fridge is in great shape. Expecting no more than a customer or two on a quiet Monday, the Chef leaves for the afternoon—just as a crowd of Chinese tourists arrives.
В холодильнике отличные улитки, я проверял.
Я не понял, что за ерунда?
Извините, пожалуйста, как у вас получится?
Let's walk back through the scene line by line.
'And I had to go buy a brand-new batch.' Max adopts a candid approach at this moment, pairing "prishlos" ("had to, it fell to") with "kupit" ("buy") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.

'You have been given a lot more authority now.' Barinov sets an earnest tempo as they talk, building the phrase around "vlasti" ("power, government") and "stalo" ("became, came over") for a crisp, natural delivery.
В холодильнике отличные улитки, я проверял.

'There are excellent snails in the fridge, I checked them myself.' Timur presents a wry stance for Barinov, combining "kholodilnike" ("fridge") and "otlichnyye" ("excellent") so the key meaning lands right away.
'Before we manage to sell it all.' Max strikes an honest approach with Timur, linking "prodadim" ("we'll sell"), "chem" ("than"), and "my" ("we") in one brisk exchange.
'Chef, where are you heading off to?' Timur asks naturally from the start, linking "kuda" ("where to"), "shef" ("Chef"), and "vy" ("you") in one brisk exchange.
'There will be at most one and a half people here today.' Timur adopts a frank mood in front of Max, leaning on "budet" ("will be") before closing the thought with "maksimum" ("maximum").
'I will be back in the evening.' Max chooses a resolute angle right away, putting "vecherom" ("in the evening") alongside "budu" ("will be") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Wait, where is everybody?' Barinov asks calmly in the room, weaving "gde" ("where") together with "vse" ("all") just the way native speakers do.
'Two huge barges.' Timur offers an unhurried position with Barinov, joining "ogromnykh" ("huge") to "barzhi" ("barge") so every word pulls its weight.
'Oh, come on now.' Max offers a resolute tack toward Timur, anchoring the Russian line on "da" ("yes") and "ladno" ("all right") without extra filler.
Я не понял, что за ерунда?
'I do not get it, what kind of nonsense is this?' Barinov asks evenly in this moment, putting "ponyal" ("understood") alongside "yerunda" ("trifle, nothing") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Oh, take it easy.' Timur sustains a firm manner without hesitation, joining "da" ("yes") to "ladno" ("all right") so every word pulls its weight.
Извините, пожалуйста, как у вас получится?
'Excuse me, please, how will you manage to seat us?' Max inquires briskly as the talk turns, weaving "izvinite" ("sorry, excuse me") together with "kak" ("how") just the way native speakers do.

That wraps up this scene as max replaces the spoiled snails just before Chef Barinov leaves for the afternoon expecting a dead Monday, right as busloads of Chinese tourists arrive at Claude Monet. See you next time!
